rows.answer:
No—each matrix being nilpotent does not imply stability under arbitrary switching. Interpreting the spoken matrices as A = [[0, a], [0, 0]] and B = [[0, 0], [b, 0]], with a, b > 0, the necessary and sufficient condition for uniform exponential stability is ab < 1.

For necessity, use the allowed alternating sequence A, B, A, B, … . Since BA = diag(0, ab), starting at x₀ = (0, 1) gives x₂ₘ = (0, (ab)ᵐ). If ab > 1, this grows exponentially. At the boundary ab = 1, it never decays, so the system is not asymptotically or uniformly exponentially stable. It is nevertheless uniformly bounded at that boundary: any product containing adjacent identical matrices is zero, and every remaining product alternates and has bounded norm.

For sufficiency, take the common diagonal quadratic Lyapunov function V(x) = p x₁² + q x₂², where p, q > 0. Direct calculation gives
V(Ax) − V(x) = −p x₁² + (p a² − q)x₂²,
V(Bx) − V(x) = (q b² − p)x₁² − q x₂².
Both differences are strictly negative for every nonzero x precisely when
p a² < q and q b² < p,
or equivalently a² < q/p < 1/b². Such positive weights exist exactly when a²b² < 1, which here means ab < 1.

Explicitly, choose p = b and q = a. Then V(Ax) ≤ ab V(x) and V(Bx) ≤ ab V(x), so every switching sequence satisfies V(xₖ) ≤ (ab)ᵏ V(x₀). Consequently,
‖xₖ‖₂ ≤ sqrt(max(a,b)/min(a,b)) · (sqrt(ab))ᵏ · ‖x₀‖₂.
This establishes a uniform exponential bound, with one-step contraction factor ab for V, or sqrt(ab) for the norm induced by V.
